name: Sornagadeswarar Temple, Neivanai (Thirunelvennai)
deity: Shiva as Sornagadeswarar (Vennaiyappar), with the Goddess Neelamalar Kanni
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, the Thirunelvennai of the Tevaram, sung by Sambandar (7th century)
summary: In the paddy country near Ulundurpet, Neivanai keeps the memory of the Lord who held back a flood with a dam of grain — the Thirunelvennai that Sambandar praised as ancient and rich in water.

sections.history: Neivanai is a small village of Ulundurpet taluk in Kallakurichi district, some 15 km from Ulundurpet, and it is the Thirunelvennai of the Tevaram. Its Shiva temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted tenth among those of Nadu Nadu, the country between the Chola and Thondai lands. Thirugnana Sambandar sang a pathigam here, preserved in the third Tirumurai, in which he speaks of Thirunelvennai as an ancient and renowned place, rich in water. The Lord's name, Sornagadeswarar, is explained from the temple's inscriptions as the Lord who granted a golden pot; the villagers also know him as Vennaiyappar.
sections.architecture: This is a modest village temple of the Nadu Nadu plain, with the Lord enshrined as a lingam in the sanctum. The Goddess, Neelamalar Kanni — she of the blue-lotus eyes — does not share his enclosure: she has her own east-facing shrine close by, almost a small temple in itself, so that worship here moves between two neighbouring sanctums.
sections.legends: The sthala purana remembers a time when the fields here were so rich that the people, secure in their grain, forgot God. Varuna sent rain without pause; tanks and lakes breached and the flood rose. Shiva came among them as a young man, had the villagers bring their sacks of paddy, and built a dam — an anai — of paddy, nel, that held back the water. From Nel-anai, tradition says, came the name Neivanai. Another story tells that Sambandar reached the village by night and could not find the way, and the Lord sent the Goddess to lead him to the temple. The Sanakadi sages too are said to have worshipped here.
sections.festivals: Karthigai Deepam in November–December, Arudra Darshanam in the month of Margazhi and Maha Shivaratri in February–March are the temple's principal observances, with the monthly pradosham kept as at every Shiva shrine; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Neivanai is a quiet farming village, and the story of a dam made of grain sits naturally among its fields. Pilgrims worship the Lord, cross to the Goddess's own east-facing shrine, and often join this visit to the other Tevaram temples of the Tirukkovilur and Ulundurpet country nearby.

visit.timings: Open in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Neivanai lies about 15 km from Ulundurpet. From Eraiyur, on the Tirukkovilur–Ulundurpet road, it is about 4 km by way of Vadakurumbur; it can also be reached by a turn off the Ulundurpet–Villupuram road. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Tiruchirappalli and Chennai are the nearest major airports.
